prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The present disclosure describes systems, methods, devices for performing thought-controlled neuromuscular stimulation. Also described are methods for producing a neuromuscular stimulation cuff. The systems and methods generally relate to receiving and processing thought signals indicative of an intended action, and then delivering stimulation to effectuate the intended action through a neuromuscular stimulation cuff. The neuromuscular stimulation cuff includes a flexible printed circuit board having at least one finger and a plurality of electrogel discs disposed on the at least one finger. The neuromuscular stimulation cuff may be produced by providing a layer of polyimide, etching a conductive copper circuit including a plurality of electrodes into the layer of polyimide to form an etched circuit layer, adhering a cover layer onto the etched circuit layer to form a flexible printed circuit board (PCB), and cutting at least one finger from the flexible PCB. The neuromuscular stimulation cuff employs a flexible multi-electrode design which allows for reanimation of complex muscle movements in a patient, including individual finger movement.

outputs.L2: This disclosure concerns devices, systems, and techniques for neuromuscular stimulation directed by a user’s thoughts, as well as processes for manufacturing a neuromuscular stimulation cuff. In general, signals representing an intended action are received and analyzed, after which the cuff applies stimulation that causes the intended movement. The cuff incorporates a flexible printed circuit board with one or more finger-like extensions, each supporting multiple electrogel discs. To manufacture the cuff, a polyimide layer may be provided, and a conductive copper circuit containing multiple electrodes may be etched into that layer to create an etched circuit layer. A cover layer is then bonded to the etched circuit layer to produce a flexible printed circuit board (PCB), from which at least one finger-like extension is cut. By using a flexible, multi-electrode configuration, the cuff can restore complex muscular actions in a patient, including movement of individual fingers.
outputs.L3:
The disclosure describes systems, methods, and devices for thought-controlled neuromuscular stimulation. Thought signals representing a user’s intended action are detected and processed to determine the desired movement. Based on this information, targeted electrical stimulation is delivered to the appropriate muscles or nerves, causing the intended movement to occur.

The neuromuscular stimulation cuff includes a flexible printed circuit board with at least one finger-shaped section. Each finger contains multiple electrogel discs that establish electrical contact with the wearer’s body and enable stimulation to be delivered at selected locations. The cuff is manufactured by etching copper electrodes into a polyimide substrate, applying a protective cover layer, and cutting finger-shaped sections from the resulting flexible circuit board.

This flexible, multi-electrode configuration allows the cuff to conform to the body while providing precise and selective stimulation. As a result, the system can reanimate complex muscle movements, including coordinated hand motion and movement of individual fingers.
outputs.L4:
The disclosure describes systems and methods for restoring voluntary movement by translating a user’s intended actions into targeted neuromuscular stimulation. Neural or physiological signals associated with an attempted or imagined movement are acquired from the user and processed to determine the intended action. A controller then converts the decoded intent into stimulation commands, including the selection of electrodes and the timing, amplitude, frequency, and duration of the electrical pulses. In this manner, the system can activate appropriate peripheral nerves or muscle groups without requiring normal signal transmission through an injured portion of the nervous system.

Electrical stimulation is delivered through a flexible, multi-electrode cuff designed to conform closely to a nerve, muscle, limb, or other anatomical structure. The cuff may be formed from an etched flexible printed circuit board comprising polyimide and copper. Multiple projecting fingers or similar compliant elements extend from the cuff and carry individually addressable electrode contacts. An electrically conductive electrogel lines or surrounds at least part of the fingers, improving contact with tissue, accommodating anatomical variation, and helping distribute stimulation current while reducing undesirable gaps or pressure points.

Because the cuff includes multiple independently controlled electrodes positioned around or along the target anatomy, stimulation can be spatially selective. Different electrode combinations and stimulation patterns may recruit distinct nerve fascicles, motor units, or muscle groups. The controller may therefore coordinate several stimulation channels to produce movements more complex than a simple contraction, such as opening or closing the hand, flexing or extending selected joints, or moving individual fingers. Stimulation parameters can be calibrated for a particular patient and adjusted to obtain the desired movement while limiting discomfort, fatigue, and unintended activation of neighboring muscles.

The system thus provides an interface between detected motor intent and the peripheral neuromuscular system. For a patient with paralysis, nerve damage, spinal cord injury, stroke-related impairment, or another condition that disrupts voluntary motor control, an attempted movement may be recognized even though the movement cannot be carried out naturally. The decoded command can then be used to stimulate the relevant neuromuscular pathways through the flexible cuff, effectively reanimating the intended motion.

By combining intent decoding with a conformable, high-density stimulation interface, the disclosed technology may enable finer and more natural control than conventional stimulation devices. In particular, the ability to recruit selected muscles or nerve pathways independently may support precise hand and finger movements needed for grasping, pinching, manipulating objects, and performing other daily tasks. The approach therefore has the potential to restore useful, individualized motor function and improve patient independence.

counterfactuals.output: A neuromuscular stimulation system is disclosed for restoring volitional movement to a limb of a subject. The system includes a neural interface configured to acquire neural signals associated with an intended movement, a processor configured to decode the neural signals into one or more movement commands, and a flexible cuff positionable around a peripheral nerve. The cuff includes a plurality of independently addressable electrodes distributed circumferentially and longitudinally along a compliant substrate. A stimulation controller selectively energizes combinations of the electrodes using stimulation parameters determined from the decoded movement commands to activate targeted nerve fascicles and produce coordinated muscle contractions. Spatial and temporal modulation of the stimulation enables complex movements, including grasping, releasing, wrist movement, and individual finger flexion or extension. In certain embodiments, sensors provide feedback indicative of limb position, applied force, muscle activity, or evoked neural response, and the processor adjusts stimulation in real time to improve movement accuracy and stability. The flexible cuff conforms to the nerve while accommodating anatomical variation and movement, thereby enabling selective, thought-controlled restoration of motor function.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe how to manufacture a flexible neuromuscular stimulation cuff using polyimide, an etched copper electrode circuit, a cover layer, and finger-shaped PCB sections, and explain its use in thought-controlled muscle reanimation.
counterfactuals.output:
A flexible neuromuscular stimulation cuff can be fabricated as a thin, patterned copper circuit laminated between polyimide layers, then divided into compliant “fingers” that conform around a peripheral nerve or muscle.

### Typical manufacturing flow

1. **Start with copper-clad polyimide**
   - Use a flexible-circuit laminate consisting of a polyimide substrate with a thin copper layer.
   - Clean and prepare the copper for photolithography.

2. **Pattern the electrode circuit**
   - Apply photoresist, expose it through a mask defining the electrodes, traces, contact pads, and routing, then develop it.
   - Etch away unwanted copper and strip the remaining resist.
   - The resulting copper pattern provides independent channels so different cuff regions can be stimulated selectively.

3. **Apply the cover layer**
   - Laminate or coat the circuit with a second polyimide “coverlay.”
   - Pattern openings over the tissue-facing electrode sites and external connector pads while leaving traces insulated.
   - Electrode windows may receive a biocompatible surface finish, such as platinum-family coatings, to improve corrosion resistance and charge-injection performance. Bare copper should not directly contact tissue.

4. **Form the finger-shaped sections**
   - Laser-cut, die-cut, or otherwise define narrow fingers in the flexible PCB outline. Each finger carries one or more exposed electrode sites.
   - The separated fingers reduce bending stiffness and allow the device to wrap around irregular anatomy without concentrating stress.
   - Add strain relief near the lead transition and connector region.

5. **Shape and package the cuff**
   - Thermoform or mechanically wrap the finger array around a mandrel approximating the target nerve or muscle geometry.
   - Incorporate a closure or compliant backing so the cuff stays positioned without compressing the tissue.
   - Attach leads or a connector, encapsulate non-electrode regions with a biocompatible barrier, and seal all copper edges.

6. **Test and validate**
   - Inspect for shorts, opens, delamination, pinholes, and exposed copper.
   - Measure electrode impedance, insulation resistance, mechanical fatigue, leakage, and electrochemical charge limits.
   - Implantable versions require validated cleaning, sterilization, biocompatibility, hermeticity, and long-term reliability testing.

### Use in thought-controlled muscle reanimation

The cuff is surgically placed around a peripheral nerve—or, in some designs, against selected muscle branches. A brain–computer interface records neural activity associated with attempted movement. Decoding software converts that activity into commands such as “open hand” or estimated joint trajectories.

A programmable stimulator then delivers **current-controlled, charge-balanced biphasic pulses** through selected cuff electrodes. By choosing channels and adjusting pulse timing, amplitude, and width, the system preferentially recruits nerve fascicles or motor branches controlling different muscles. Coordinated stimulation can restore functions such as grasping, wrist extension, standing, or stepping.

In a closed-loop system, sensors measuring limb position, force, muscle activity, or contact provide feedback so stimulation can be corrected in real time. The brain signal supplies the user’s intent; the cuff acts as the output interface that converts that intent into muscle contraction. Because excessive current, net DC charge, pressure, or heating can injure nerves and tissue, implantation and programming must be performed as part of a professionally designed and regulated medical system.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a patent abstract for a brain-controlled functional electrical stimulation device capable of reanimating complex muscle movements through a flexible cuff containing multiple electrodes and electrogel discs.
counterfactuals.output: A brain-controlled functional electrical stimulation system for reanimating coordinated muscle movement includes a neural signal acquisition device, a controller, and a flexible stimulation cuff configured for placement around a limb or body region. The cuff carries an array of independently addressable electrodes, each electrode being coupled to an electrogel disc that conforms to the skin and provides a low-impedance stimulation interface. The controller processes brain signals to identify an intended movement and generates spatially and temporally coordinated stimulation patterns for selectively activating multiple muscles or motor points. Electrode amplitude, pulse width, frequency, polarity, and activation timing may be independently adjusted to produce complex movements, including grasping, reaching, standing, or walking. Sensors may provide feedback regarding limb position, muscle activity, cuff contact, or generated force, enabling closed-loop adaptation of stimulation parameters. The flexible cuff supports repeatable electrode positioning while accommodating anatomical variation and movement, thereby facilitating personalized restoration or assistance of motor function.
